title: Measuring improvements over the base model

opening.headline: Let's find out under what conditions we can compare and show that the tuned model is better than the basic model.
body: Tuning has costs associated with data preparation, training, and operations. To justify the cost, there must be evidence that it is better than the basic model, and the impression that “it was good when I used it” is not grounds. You must first decide what to compare and under what conditions.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the concepts of the baseline and the same evaluation set as the starting point for comparison, the reasons for comparing the tuning model to the basic model of the improved prompt, and the perspectives on whether the difference in averages is a coincidence. Next, the instructor's commentary explains cases where improvement has been inflated and cases broken down by type.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The conditions for comparing two models can be distinguished using the same evaluation set.
You can determine the size and confidence level of improvement

screens.title: Must show that the tuned model is better than the base model
screens.lead: Read about who needs to report tuning results. It's a good idea to read it while thinking about what kind of evidence you need.

paragraphs: One team spent several weeks preparing data and tuning the model. Now the person in charge has to show that this tune-up was worth the cost. This is because tuning costs money, from data preparation and training to subsequent operations.

It is not a basis for saying, “I tried it and it was good.” This is because each person remembers different cases, and a few things that went well stand out more. The justification for costs must be comparable numbers.

To do this, you must first decide what to compare and under what conditions. The conditions are which model to use as a standard, which input and which grader to measure, and how to confirm that the difference is not a coincidence. This class organizes these three things one by one.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you only compare your tuned model to the baseline model in its original state, the effects of tuning may appear larger than they really are. We will find out why during class.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the state of records so far.

screens.title: Recall: Did you record the evaluation values of the base model before tuning?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Did you record the evaluation values of the base model before tuning?
items.answer: Without records, it is impossible to say how much improvement there is. Even if the value after tuning looks good, if there is no object to compare it to, it is impossible to know whether the value is high. Before starting tuning, it is important to reset the current state first.

items.prompt: Were there also evaluation values for the base model that improved the prompts?
items.answer: It is important that you have sufficiently refined your prompt before considering tuning. Since improving prompts is often enough, the base model with improved prompts is the real comparison.

items.prompt: What input and grader was used for the evaluation?
items.answer: When evaluating a tuning model, if the input or scoring criteria are different, the two values cannot be placed side by side. Same input and same scorer are prerequisites for comparison.

screens.outro: Let’s check the baseline and the same evaluation set as the starting point for comparison.

screens.title: Same evaluation set as baseline
screens.lead: Click the next button to check the conditions for a fair comparison one by one.

visual.alt: An illustration showing the comparison between the baseline model and the tuning model using the same evaluation set and the same scorer.
labels: Evaluation value A / Evaluation value B

steps.title: baseline
steps.body: The baseline is the evaluation value measured before the change. All comparisons start here. Without a baseline, it is impossible to tell whether the value has increased after tuning or whether it was at that level originally.

steps.title: Same evaluation set
steps.body: Baseline and tuning models must be evaluated with the same inputs, the same scorer, and the same criteria. If the evaluation set or scoring criteria are different, it is impossible to know whether the difference in values ​​is due to the model or the evaluation conditions.

steps.title: Holdouts as control group
steps.body: Before you start tuning, set aside some of the data you have collected. This holdout is not used for training, but serves as a control group in the evaluation. Training and holdout should have roughly the same variety of input types and responses.

steps.title: View indicators and statistics together
steps.body: If you upload training and test files together when submitting a training job, you can receive statistics on both while training is in progress. This statistic is a signal that tells you whether the model is improving, and after training is completed, it is measured again using an evaluation service or an evaluation you created yourself.

steps.title: Repeat with the same criteria for each change
steps.body: Evaluation doesn't just happen once. Whenever you change the prompt, change data, or change hyperparameters, you need to record them repeatedly using the same criteria so you can know which change had what effect.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at which model we should compare to to see if it's fair.

screens.title: Comparison with Prompt Improvements
screens.lead: Select each tab to see which base model your tuning model should be compared to and why.

tabs.label: Why prompt first?
tabs.body: Prompt engineering is the best first step in establishing a baseline. Starting with a simple prompt and expected output and adding context, instructions, and examples defines what accuracy means for this task and reveals why it is incorrect. For many tasks, prompts are sufficient, such as summarizing, translating, and generating code.

tabs.label: The right comparison point
tabs.body: Tuned models should be compared to the baseline model with improved prompts, not to the baseline model in its original state. Comparing only weak prompts before tuning inflates the amount of improvement, and the difference may have been achieved simply by improving the prompts rather than tuning.

tabs.label: different levers
tabs.body: Tuning, searching, and prompting are levers to solve different problems. Contextual optimization increases response accuracy when the model does not know the information, is out of date, or requires in-house information. Model optimization increases consistency of behavior when formatting, tone, or reasoning are inconsistent. Only when the evaluation results show which side of the problem is the problem can you choose a lever.

tabs.label: cost benefit
tabs.body: By training the model to learn the contents of long prompts through tuning, the prompts can be reduced, and the token cost can be reduced accordingly. In addition to the improvement, this gain is also calculated and compared. However, if you repeat the instructions for each learning example, it is easy to obtain good results even with a small amount of data, so the choice to reduce prompts is made after confirmation through evaluation.

screens.outro: Now that you've decided on a comparison, let's consider whether the differences are believable.

screens.title: Confidence level of statistical difference and improvement
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the mean differences should be interpreted depending on the size and repetition of the evaluation set.

stops.body: Even if there is a difference in means, it may be a coincidence if the evaluation set is small. For example, if you get two or three more correct answers out of 20, it is difficult to determine which one did well. The larger the evaluation set, the more reliable differences of the same size become.

Model output is non-deterministic, meaning the results may fluctuate even with the same input. If you judge based on the results of one spin, your luck will be mixed. Repeat the same assessment several times to see how scattered the results are.

Check whether the difference between the two models is large enough to outweigh the scatter in the repeated results. If the scatter is large but the difference is small, it is likely to be a coincidence, and if the scatter is small but the difference is large, it is reliable.

Instead of just looking at the overall average, we break down which input types won. The average may go up only slightly but it may be significantly better in certain types, or the average may go up but it gets worse in important types.

Whether improved accuracy is worth the cost is measured by the cost of failure. Failure to misinform a customer that their refund will be $1,000 instead of $100 is much more expensive than one awkward sentence. How accurate is enough is determined by the costs of failure and the benefits of success.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to the case.

screens.title: Case Description: When the tuning model is similar to the base model in an improved prompt
screens.lead: The instructor interprets the results of the hypothetical comparison. Click the Next button to see how your initial conclusion changes.

steps.title: first result
steps.body: When we compared the tuned model with the original basic model on the same evaluation set, it was significantly ahead. The team decided that tuning was successful and attempted to write an introduction report.

steps.title: change the object of comparison
steps.body: At that time, a team member suggested that we re-evaluate the basic model of the improvement prompt with clear instructions and examples using the same evaluation set. The results showed little difference from the tuned model.

steps.title: interpretation
steps.body: The initial big difference was due to the weak pre-tuning prompt. The amount of improvement was inflated, and in reality, the additional benefit from tuning alone was small.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: If tuning involves data preparation, training, and operational costs, you may decide that the additional benefit is not worth it. This judgment was made possible by re-establishing the baseline with improved prompts.

steps.title: remaining calculations
steps.body: Still, it's worth calculating separately whether tuning can lower token costs by reducing long prompts. Services with a high number of calls may benefit from fewer prompts. This gain is listed as a single line in the comparison table, independent of the amount of improvement. Conversely, if the tuned model has a higher call cost than the base model with longer prompts, you should also calculate whether the reduced token cost offsets the price difference. The comparison table organized in this way becomes the basis for decision makers to decide whether to continue tuning.

screens.outro: This time, let’s break down what the average covers by type.

screens.title: Case study: Improvements broken down by type
screens.lead: When you select each item, the instructor's commentary unfolds. Check out what the average covers by type.

items.prompt: The overall average has only risen slightly, but what do we see by type?
items.answer: In the hypothetical case, the types of formatting errors were greatly reduced, while the types of questions asking for facts remained the same. In the overall average, the two changes were mixed and the improvement seemed small.

items.prompt: What do these results mean that tuning is effective for?
items.answer: Tuning is effective at ensuring consistency of behavior, such as format or tone, and does not fill in knowledge that the model does not know. The evaluation results demonstrate this distinction.

items.prompt: In fact, the question is, how can we improve it?
items.answer: When it comes to lack of knowledge, it is better to provide the necessary information in context through search. In fact, the accuracy of the question may not increase significantly even if more tuning data is collected.

items.prompt: How do we connect this conclusion to the next step?
items.answer: Divide and determine which lever is needed for which type, and record the results to use as a hypothesis for the next iteration. The cycle of evaluation, hypothesis, application, and reassessment is the basic unit of improvement.

items.prompt: How can tuning data be utilized in this case?
items.answer: It is very effective if you reinforce it by focusing on examples of types with formatting errors. By adding examples targeting weaker types and comparing before and after changes using the same evaluation set, you can see whether your reinforcement actually worked. Conversely, ineffective fact question types are separated into a separate improvement task that adds context through search.

items.prompt: How do I include the results by type in the report?
items.answer: Instead of just writing down the overall average, write down the baseline value and post-tuning value for each type side by side. It becomes easier to make subsequent decisions when it becomes clear which types have improved and which types remain the same. You can also write down the size of the evaluation set and the number of iterations so the reader can gauge the level of confidence in the differences.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We outline how to measure improvements over the baseline model. As you read, think of your baseline.

paragraphs: The starting point for comparison is the baseline. Before starting tuning, reset the current state and compare before and after changes using the same evaluation set and the same scorer. The evaluation set comes from holdouts that were not used for training.

The tuning model is compared not to the initial state, but to a base model that has sufficiently improved the prompt. Only then will the additional benefits of tuning be revealed. Whether the difference is coincidental is examined by evaluation set size, repetition, and decomposition by type.
Finally, the magnitude of improvement is read together with the cost of failure. The decision is based on whether the numbers justify the cost, rather than the fact that the numbers have gone up.
Going back to the original question, the evidence that tuning is better is only convincing when three things are in place: comparison with a baseline, the same evaluation set, and improved prompts.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: If the evaluation results after tuning are different from expectations, check the data, and if they are the same even after the data has been cleaned, reconsider the method or task definition.

checks.intro: Think of the principles for deciding what to compare. Just choose the most appropriate comparison object.
checks.q: What is the most appropriate comparison when judging the effectiveness of a tuned model?
options: The basic model in its original state without any modifications to the prompts.
Previous run results between tuning models
Impression of seeing only user reactions without evaluation
checks.explain: Comparing only the weak prompts before tuning will inflate the amount of improvement. To justify the tuning cost, the improved prompt should be compared to the baseline model on the same evaluation set.

wrong.0: Compared to a baseline model with weak prompts, the benefits of tuning are overestimated.
wrong.1: Comparisons between tuning models do not provide evidence for gains over the base model.
wrong.3: Impressions are unfounded and must be compared with the same evaluation set and grader.

checks.correctFeedback: Good. Only by comparing it with the best basic model can the benefits of tuning be revealed.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Rethink what comparison you can make that doesn't inflate the tuning gains.

checks.intro: For each problem situation, try connecting the lever you want to pull first. Just pair the situation on the left with the action on the right.
checks.q: Match the problem situation with the lever you want to pull first.
left: The model keeps getting wrong when asked questions about facts it doesn’t know.
There is a lot of room for improvement if instructions are clear and examples are provided.
right: Establish a baseline first by improving prompts
Search provides necessary information in context
checks.explain: Tuning addresses behavioral axes like consistency, retrieval addresses information axes, and improving prompting is the best first step in establishing a baseline.
checks.correctFeedback: We chose the right lever for all three situations.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some things are out of sync. First try to determine whether the problem is consistency of behavior, lack of information, or lack of a baseline yet.

glossary.def: This is the evaluation value measured in the state before the change and is the starting point for all comparisons.
The evaluation input and scoring criteria are the same for all candidates being compared.
This is evaluation data set aside rather than used for learning.
It is a difference in size that is difficult to attribute to coincidence.

misconceptions.myth: As long as the tuned model is better than the original base model, it is a success.
misconceptions.fact: Only when compared to the base model with improved prompts is the additional benefit of tuning revealed.

misconceptions.myth: If the average rises, it is an improvement.
misconceptions.fact: Unless you look at the size of the evaluation set and the variations in output, it could be a coincidence. Check it by dividing it by type.

misconceptions.myth: It is convenient to create a separate evaluation set for each model.
misconceptions.fact: Comparisons can only be made if the evaluation set and scorer are the same. If the conditions are different, the cause of the difference is unknown.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The comparison is to the best baseline model.
Compare with the same evaluation set and the same scorer.
Note the baseline before making any changes.
The size of the difference and trust are judged together.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is our baseline, is it the value of the base model that sufficiently improves the prompt?
